analysis.one_liner: Lets individual workers sign private contracts with employers, bypassing union representation.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee; it died at the end of the 102nd Congress with no vote ever taken.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal labor law so that any single employee could opt out of union representation and sign an individual employment contract directly with the employer, overriding any existing union contract. Introduced by Rep. Richard Armey with one Republican cosponsor, it was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat. No vote was ever held, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers at workplaces with union contracts would gain the ability to strike separate deals with individual workers, letting them hire or retain employees on terms outside the collective bargaining agreement. Individual workers who prefer to negotiate alone could do so.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers seeking alternatives to union contracts

how_it_helps.text: Any individual employee could elect to enter into and administer an employment contract directly with the employer, without the bargaining representative intervening.
The individual contract would take effect notwithstanding any other provision of the law or any collective-bargaining contract, meaning it would override existing union agreements.

analysis.who_pays: Workers at unionized workplaces would bear the cost if enough colleagues opted out: bargaining units shrink, union dues and leverage fall, and the collectively bargained wages and benefits that apply to everyone become harder to win and maintain. Unions would lose members and bargaining power.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unionized workers and their bargaining representatives

drawbacks.text: The bill would let employers negotiate separate deals that undercut a collectively bargained contract, weakening the bargaining position of the workers who remain in the unit.

Workers who wanted to negotiate individually would lose the legal protections and leverage that come with union representation, since the bill removes the bargaining representative from the process entirely.

A fair-minded objection is that some employees genuinely prefer individual arrangements and dislike being bound by a union contract they did not personally negotiate; this bill would give them that choice, but at the risk of unraveling contracts covering co-workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the individual worker who wants out of a union contract, the bill offers real freedom of choice. But the mechanism is one where each opt-out weakens the contract that protects the rest, and employers gain the ability to bargain people out of collective terms one at a time. On balance the bill's design favors employers over the workforce as a whole.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to committee and a subcommittee, but no vote or further action ever happened before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Armey introduced the bill in the House on May 4, 1992, and it was referred to the Committee on Education and Labor the same day.
On May 12, 1992, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations, where it remained.
The bill had one cosponsor, a Republican, and no further action was recorded before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Unionized workers and their unions are better off, because the bill that would have allowed individual contracts to override collective bargaining agreements never advanced. Employers who would have benefited from negotiating around union contracts gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Richard K. Armey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let individual employees contract directly with employers, bypassing union representation.

for.name: 1 House Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it attracted no other sponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 4, 1992, and referred it to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations; the committee never took it up for action or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republicans were attached to the bill (the sponsor and one cosponsor), and the Democratic-controlled committee that held it never acted on it; no vote was ever held to measure broader support.

industries.note: The bill would let any member opt out of representation, draining unions of members, dues, and bargaining leverage. Unions bargain for wages and conditions covering all workers in the unit, so their interest runs alongside most workers' here.

Employers could sign individual contracts that override the collective bargaining agreement, giving them a way to set terms worker by worker. The saving for the employer comes out of the collectively bargained terms the workforce depends on.
